introduction-its-not-about-the-flops.core: Modern AI performance is often limited by moving data rather than raw compute: memory bandwidth (HBM), GPU-to-GPU links (NVLink) and node-to-node networks (InfiniBand/RoCE). The topology, the 'plumbing', decides how fast models train and serve.

first_principles.problem: A cluster with the fastest GPUs trains slowly because gradients crawl across a slow network.
truths: Compute has outpaced memory and network bandwidth.
Distributed training is communication-heavy.
Bottlenecks move to the slowest link.
derivation: Use **NVLink/NVSwitch** inside nodes and **InfiniBand/RoCE** between them.

analogy.title: A factory with fast workers and a slow conveyor belt
analogy.story: The fastest workers in the world still wait if the belt brings parts slowly.
analogy.breaks: Some workloads are genuinely compute-bound, where more FLOPS do help.

example.title: Same GPUs, different interconnects
flow: 8 nodes × 8 GPUs over 25 Gb Ethernet: 10 days
Same GPUs over 400 Gb InfiniBand: 3 days
example.outcome: you can see topology as performance.

check.q: Why can AI training be bottlenecked by networks rather than GPUs?
check.a: Distributed training exchanges huge amounts of data (gradients), so slow links leave fast GPUs waiting.

hbm-high-bandwidth-memory-the-firehose.core: GPUs use HBM: memory stacked vertically next to the GPU die on an interposer, with very wide buses giving terabytes per second (H100 ~3.35 TB/s) versus about 100 GB/s for DDR. It feeds thousands of cores but is limited in capacity and expensive.

first_principles.problem: Ordinary DDR RAM can't supply data fast enough to keep thousands of GPU cores busy.
truths: Wide, short connections give high bandwidth.
Stacking memory saves space and distance.
Capacity and cost trade against bandwidth.

analogy.title: A firehose vs. a garden hose
analogy.story: Both carry water, but the firehose delivers vastly more per second.
analogy.breaks: Even HBM can be the bottleneck for memory-bound work like LLM decoding.

example.title: Bandwidth comparison

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: GPU cores can actually be fed.

example.outcome: you understand why GPU memory is special.

check.q: Why do GPUs use HBM instead of standard DDR memory?
check.a: HBM provides much higher bandwidth (TB/s) to feed thousands of parallel cores.

the-hbm-bottleneck-memory-bound-vs-compu.core: Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved) decides the bottleneck. Compute-bound work (large matrix multiplies in training) uses many FLOPs per byte; memory-bound work (LLM token decoding, small batches) moves lots of data for few FLOPs, so bandwidth limits it. The roofline model visualises this.

first_principles.problem: Teams buy GPUs with more FLOPS for LLM inference, which is actually limited by memory bandwidth.
truths: Each operation needs data movement.
Low reuse of data means bandwidth limits speed.
Batching raises arithmetic intensity.
derivation: Use the **roofline**: below the ridge → memory-bound.
Raise intensity with **batching**, **quantisation** and kernel fusion.

analogy.title: A chef chopping vs. fetching
analogy.story: If each dish needs one quick chop but a long walk to the fridge, the walking (memory) limits speed, not the chopping.
analogy.breaks: Real workloads mix phases (LLM prefill is compute-bound, decode memory-bound).

example.title: LLM inference phases
flow: Decode (one token at a time): reload weights each step → memory-bound
Batch many requests → decode becomes more efficient

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Optimise the bottleneck that actually applies.

example.outcome: hardware decisions based on workload type.

check.q: Why is LLM token decoding typically memory-bound?
check.a: Each new token requires reading the model weights from memory for relatively little computation, so bandwidth limits speed.

topology-level-1-nvlink-and-nvswitch-int.core: Inside a server, GPUs communicate over NVLink (direct GPU-to-GPU links, around 900 GB/s on H100) rather than PCIe (~64 GB/s). NVSwitch connects all GPUs at full bandwidth, letting 8 GPUs behave almost like one big GPU for tensor parallelism.

first_principles.problem: A model split across 8 GPUs over PCIe spends most of its time waiting for inter-GPU transfers.
truths: PCIe bandwidth is limited and shared.
Tensor parallelism communicates every layer.
Direct links avoid the CPU.
derivation: **NVSwitch**: all-to-all at full bandwidth inside the node.
Keep **tensor parallelism inside a node** (NVLink domain).

analogy.title: Coworkers at one table vs. across town
analogy.story: Passing notes across a table is instant; mailing them across town is slow.
analogy.breaks: NVLink domains are limited in size (typically 8 GPUs, larger in GB200 NVL72), so beyond that you need networks.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The most chatty communication stays on the fastest links.

check.q: Why should tensor parallelism stay within one NVLink/NVSwitch node?
check.a: It communicates at every layer, needing the very high bandwidth that only intra-node GPU links provide.

topology-level-2-ethernet-vs-infiniband-.core: Across nodes, AI clusters use InfiniBand (low latency, RDMA-native, lossless, the HPC standard) or high-speed Ethernet with RoCE (RDMA over converged Ethernet, which needs lossless configuration). Per-GPU bandwidth (400–800 Gb/s) and topology (fat-tree, rail-optimised) determine scaling.

first_principles.problem: Standard data-centre Ethernet with TCP adds latency and CPU overhead that cripples multi-node training.
truths: Distributed training needs high bandwidth and low latency.
Packet loss hurts RDMA performance.
Network topology affects congestion.
derivation: **InfiniBand**: RDMA built in, credit-based lossless flow.
**RoCEv2**: RDMA over Ethernet with PFC/ECN tuning.

analogy.title: A dedicated express rail line vs. city streets
analogy.story: Express rail (InfiniBand) moves freight without traffic lights; city streets (plain Ethernet) have congestion and stops.
analogy.breaks: InfiniBand is costly and specialised, while Ethernet (Ultra Ethernet) is catching up.

example.title: Cluster network design
flow: 8× 400 Gb NICs per node (one per GPU)

check.q: What does RoCE stand for, and why does it matter?
check.a: RDMA over Converged Ethernet, which brings low-latency, CPU-bypassing RDMA to Ethernet networks for AI clusters.

the-all-reduce-operation-why-network-top.core: In data-parallel training every GPU computes gradients on its own batch, then all GPUs must average them (all-reduce) before the next step. Ring and tree all-reduce algorithms (NCCL) move about 2× the gradient size per GPU per step, so network bandwidth directly limits step time.

first_principles.problem: Adding more GPUs doesn't speed up training because the gradient synchronisation takes longer than the computation.
truths: Every step needs synchronised gradients.
Communication volume scales with model size.
The slowest link bounds the collective.

analogy.title: A synchronised dance
analogy.story: Every dancer must finish their move and sync with all others before the next beat, so the slowest pass sets the tempo.
analogy.breaks: Very large models use other parallelisms (tensor, pipeline, ZeRO) with different communication patterns.

example.title: Communication time estimate
flow: At 400 Gb/s (~50 GB/s) vs 25 Gb/s (~3 GB/s): 16x difference

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The network choice decides scaling efficiency.

example.outcome: you understand why topology drives training speed.

check.q: What does all-reduce do in data-parallel training?
check.a: It combines (averages) gradients from all GPUs so every replica applies the same update.

gpu-direct-rdma-eliminating-the-cpu-from.core: Normally GPU-to-remote-GPU data goes GPU → CPU memory → NIC → network → NIC → CPU memory → GPU. GPUDirect RDMA lets the NIC read and write GPU memory directly, removing extra copies and CPU involvement, which cuts latency and frees the CPU.

first_principles.problem: Extra copies through host memory add latency and saturate CPU and memory bandwidth during training.
truths: Each copy costs time and bandwidth.
RDMA NICs can access memory directly.
PCIe topology affects peer-to-peer paths.
derivation: Place **NIC and GPU** on the same PCIe switch/NUMA node.

analogy.title: Direct delivery vs. a sorting office
analogy.story: Instead of routing every parcel through a central sorting office, couriers deliver door to door.
analogy.breaks: It needs compatible hardware, drivers and topology, and misconfiguration silently falls back to the slow path.

example.title: Verifying the fast path

code.text:
NCCL_DEBUG=INFO all_reduce_perf -b 1G -e 4G -g 8
# look for: NET/IB ... GPU Direct RDMA enabled

example.outcome: the shortest data path between GPUs.

check.q: What does GPUDirect RDMA eliminate from the data path?
check.a: Copies through CPU host memory, letting the NIC access GPU memory directly.
